paragraphs: A Markov chain evolves through random transitions, and convergence analysis asks how quickly its distribution approaches stationarity. This matters for stochastic systems and optimization, but traditional mathematical techniques can produce bounds that are difficult to use for realistic chains. This paper introduces the Deep Contractive Drift Calculator, or DCDC, to compute convergence bounds from samples.

The approach connects a mathematical equation with a neural network solver. The authors introduce the Contractive Drift Equation, whose solution yields an explicit convergence bound measured in Wasserstein distance. They then develop a neural network method for solving that equation. The network therefore supports a specific mathematical route from sampled behavior to a bound on convergence.

The paper analyzes how many samples the algorithm needs and demonstrates it on chains arising from stochastic processing networks and optimization with a constant step size. These examples show how the framework can produce bounds for realistic applications. Its contribution is to make convergence analysis computationally approachable while retaining an explicit connection between the equation being solved and the resulting guarantee.
neurips-2024-deep-learning-for-computing.tldr: DCDC uses a neural network to solve an equation that yields explicit bounds on how quickly Markov chains approach stationarity.

paragraphs: An anomaly detector can flag unusual activity without labeled examples of attacks, yet leave users unable to understand its decisions. This paper develops a way to express those decisions as interpretable rules. Its focus is on understanding the structure of normal data and the boundaries separating normal observations from anomalies.

The method first uses a Segmentation Clustering Decision Tree to divide the data into regions. Predictions from the original anomaly detector help determine the tree's splits, so the segmentation reflects information from the model being explained. A Gaussian Boundary Delineation algorithm then fits boundaries within the resulting regions, providing a more detailed distinction between normal and anomalous points.

Together, segmentation and flexible boundary fitting are intended to address high dimensionality and maintain resilience to data drift and perturbations. The resulting boundaries are translated into a collection of understandable rules. Across the datasets and models evaluated, the authors report better explanation accuracy, agreement with the original detector, and robustness than existing methods. These findings concern how faithfully and reliably the rules explain the detector's behavior.
neurips-2024-dissect-black-box-interpret.tldr: A model-guided decision tree and locally fitted boundaries turn black-box anomaly detection decisions into interpretable rules.

paragraphs: Rendering a moving scene requires representing both its appearance and how it changes over time. Gaussian splatting offers high rendering quality at real-time speeds, motivating approaches that deform a shared collection of three-dimensional Gaussians to represent individual frames. This paper targets two problems in that setup: noisy coordinates and insufficient use of information across space and time.

DN-4DGS introduces a noise suppression strategy that changes the coordinate distribution of the shared Gaussians. The purpose is to reduce the noise that those coordinates can pass into the deformation model. A separate temporal-spatial aggregation module collects information from nearby points and adjacent frames, giving the model access to related observations when representing dynamic changes.

The two components address different parts of the rendering process: the quality of the underlying coordinates and the information available to model their evolution. Experiments on several real-world datasets report state-of-the-art rendering quality while maintaining real-time operation. The stated result is therefore a combination of visual quality and speed, with noise handling and aggregation contributing to the proposed dynamic-scene framework.
neurips-2024-dn-4dgs-denoised-deformable.tldr: DN-4DGS combines coordinate noise suppression with information from nearby points and frames to improve real-time dynamic-scene rendering.

paragraphs: Distributed training can reduce communication by compressing gradients before transmitting them. Existing analyses considered sampling gradients with replacement, whereas random reshuffling uses sampling without replacement. This paper studies the combination of compression and random reshuffling, addressing a gap between communication-saving techniques and a sampling approach with established practical and theoretical advantages.

The authors first introduce Q-RR, a distributed random-reshuffling method with gradient compression. They use control iterates to reduce the variance introduced by gradient quantization. The central concern is that saving communication also introduces noise, so the algorithm needs a mechanism for managing that noise alongside the reshuffling procedure.

The paper then adapts the approach to federated learning through Q-NASTYA, which incorporates local gradient updates and separate local and global step sizes. It also develops compression-variance reduction for this setting. The authors prove convergence results and identify several settings where the proposed methods improve on existing algorithms. Those improvements are tied to the analyzed settings, while the broader contribution is a framework for studying compressed communication together with without-replacement sampling and local computation.
neurips-2024-don-t-compress-gradients-in.tldr: The paper develops and analyzes compressed random-reshuffling methods, including a federated variant, with mechanisms to reduce compression noise.

paragraphs: Code generated by a language model can be inefficient, taking longer to run and consuming more memory than necessary. EffiLearner addresses this by giving the model feedback from actual execution. Its goal is to improve generated programs through repeated measurement and revision, using observed overhead to guide the next version.

The framework starts by asking a language model to generate code. It runs that code locally and records profiles of execution time and memory usage. Those profiles are then returned to the model, which revises the program to reduce overhead. Repeating this process connects optimization decisions to the program's measured behavior.

The authors evaluate EffiLearner on EffiBench and two additional code-generation benchmarks using 16 open-source and six closed-source models. They report substantial efficiency improvements through iteration. For StarCoder2-15B on EffiBench, execution time falls from 0.93 to 0.12 seconds, while total memory usage falls from 22.02 to 2.03 megabyte-seconds. The latter measures memory consumption across execution time. These results illustrate how execution feedback can improve resource use for the evaluated generated programs.
neurips-2024-effilearner-enhancing-effic.tldr: EffiLearner repeatedly feeds execution-time and memory profiles back to language models to improve the efficiency of their generated code.

paragraphs: A generative model may learn an underlying concept before ordinary prompts reveal that ability. This paper investigates that possibility by tracking learning in a concept space, where each axis represents an independent concept in the process that generates the data. This makes it possible to examine which concepts are learned and in what order.

The authors identify properties of the data, called concept signal, that control the speed of concept learning and therefore its order. They also observe abrupt changes in the direction of learning within concept space. In their experiments, these turns coincide with hidden capabilities becoming detectable through interventions in the model's internal representation, even though naive input prompting cannot yet elicit them.

The findings come from synthetically constructed toy datasets, which provide the setting for identifying these concepts and tracking their development. The authors hypothesize that a broader pattern may hold for generative models: latent capabilities could emerge suddenly and consistently before appearing through simple prompts. The distinction matters because observed prompting performance may lag behind the capabilities revealed by internal interventions in the studied models.
neurips-2024-emergence-of-hidden-capabil.tldr: On synthetic toy datasets, changes in learning trajectories reveal internal concept capabilities before naive prompts can elicit them.

paragraphs: Topic modeling seeks to uncover themes in a collection of documents. Existing methods can struggle to combine useful topics with efficient and stable operation. FASTopic proposes a framework that discovers topics by modeling semantic relationships among document representations, topic representations, and word representations.

Its central mechanism, Dual Semantic-relation Reconstruction, uses document embeddings produced by a pretrained Transformer alongside learnable topic and word embeddings. Reconstructing relationships among these representations allows hidden topics to emerge. This organizes topic discovery around the semantic connections between documents, topics, and words, providing the basis for the paper's compact and efficient modeling approach.

The authors also introduce an Embedding Transport Plan to regulate those relationships using optimal transport plans. This component addresses a bias problem in how the semantic relations are formed, supporting more effective topic modeling. Across benchmark experiments and different scenarios, FASTopic is reported to outperform state-of-the-art baselines in effectiveness, efficiency, adaptability, stability, and transferability. The findings support the combined design: Transformer document representations supply semantic information, while reconstruction and transport-based regulation shape that information into topics.
neurips-2024-fastopic-pretrained-transfo.tldr: FASTopic discovers topics by reconstructing semantic relationships among Transformer document embeddings and learnable topic and word embeddings.

paragraphs: Co-crystallization offers a way to modify the physical and chemical properties of organic crystals. This paper focuses on tabletability, a property important to pharmaceutical development. It introduces GEMCODE, an automated screening and design pipeline intended to generate new co-crystal candidates with desired tabletability profiles.

GEMCODE combines deep generative models with evolutionary optimization to explore the target chemical space more broadly. The generative and optimization components form a hybrid search process directed toward the desired material properties. This connects candidate creation with a specific pharmaceutical design objective, making the pipeline relevant to the search for crystals that can better meet tablet-manufacturing needs.

The authors report experimental studies covering validation and discovery cases, finding the approach effective under realistic computational constraints. They also investigate the potential of language models for co-crystal generation and present numerous previously unknown co-crystals predicted by GEMCODE. These predictions are proposed candidates, while accelerated drug development is discussed as a potential application. The work's stated contribution is an efficient route for exploring co-crystal designs with targeted properties.
neurips-2024-hybrid-generative-ai-for-de.tldr: GEMCODE combines generative models and evolutionary optimization to propose co-crystals with targeted tabletability properties.

paragraphs: Evidential deep learning estimates uncertainty alongside classification probabilities, supporting detection of inputs outside the training distribution. This paper argues that its usual evidence representation is too restrictive because it assigns support only to individual categories. Evidence that could support several known categories collectively is omitted, weakening uncertainty estimates and out-of-distribution detection.

Hyper-opinion Evidential Deep Learning expands the representation to include both sharp evidence for one category and vague evidence compatible with multiple categories. An opinion projection mechanism then translates this richer representation into a multinomial opinion that can be optimized within the evidential learning framework. This provides a route from collective evidence to classification and uncertainty outputs.

The paper also addresses vanishing gradients in fully connected layers, reporting that the projection mechanism mitigates this problem without adding model complexity. Experiments across many datasets show better out-of-distribution detection than existing methods. The approach matters because it treats ambiguity among familiar categories as information to represent explicitly, while connecting that richer evidence representation to both uncertainty estimation and the optimization process used for classification.
neurips-2024-hyper-opinion-evidential-de.tldr: HEDL represents evidence for both individual and multiple categories to improve uncertainty estimation and out-of-distribution detection.

paragraphs: Expected calibration error, or ECE, evaluates how well a model's confidence corresponds to its predictive performance. It groups predictions into bins, but this estimation procedure can introduce bias. The paper analyzes that bias for two common strategies: bins with roughly equal numbers of observations and bins covering equal-width confidence intervals.

The authors derive upper bounds on estimation bias with an improved convergence rate. Their bounds also identify an optimal number of bins for minimizing that bias. This makes the choice of bin count part of the theoretical analysis, helping explain how the measurement procedure itself affects the calibration estimate.

The work then extends from estimation bias to generalization using an information-theoretic approach. The resulting upper bounds support numerical assessment of ECE on unknown data. Experiments with deep learning models produce nonvacuous bounds, meaning the guarantees provide informative constraints in the evaluated settings. Together, the results connect the construction of the calibration metric with the question of how reliably it describes performance beyond the data used in the analysis.
neurips-2024-information-theoretic-gener.tldr: The paper bounds bias in binned calibration estimates and derives informative generalization bounds for expected calibration error.

paragraphs: CLIP represents information using dense, high-dimensional vectors that work well across multimodal tasks but are difficult to interpret. SpLiCE seeks to make those representations understandable by expressing them through human-readable semantic concepts. It uses structure already present in CLIP's latent space to support this transformation.

The authors frame the task as sparse recovery: finding a small collection of concepts whose weighted combination represents a CLIP embedding. The resulting sparse linear representation exposes which concepts contribute, giving users a more interpretable description of information otherwise distributed across many numerical dimensions. The method is task-agnostic and requires no training.

The paper reports that these concept representations can explain existing CLIP embeddings and can also replace the dense representations while maintaining high downstream performance. Demonstrated uses include identifying spurious correlations and editing models. These applications show why an interpretable representation can be operationally useful: the concepts provide a basis for examining and modifying what a model represents. The stated contribution therefore combines transparency with continued usefulness in downstream applications.
neurips-2024-interpreting-clip-with-spar.tldr: SpLiCE converts CLIP embeddings into sparse combinations of understandable concepts without training, supporting interpretation and model editing.

paragraphs: Assessing a point cloud's perceptual quality without a pristine reference requires distinguishing what the scene contains from how it has been distorted. The paper argues that existing models mix those two kinds of information in one network, overlooking their different roles. DisPA addresses this through separate representations for content and distortion.

The framework uses two encoder branches with different inputs and training strategies. The content branch is pretrained with masked auto-encoding to capture semantic information from rendered images of distorted point clouds. The distortion branch receives a mini-patch map designed to focus attention on local, low-level distortion patterns. These choices encourage the branches to specialize.

DisPA also explicitly minimizes the mutual information between the two representations, using an estimator of a tight upper bound on their actual mutual information. Reducing this objective encourages less shared information between content and distortion. Experiments across multiple point-cloud quality datasets report performance above state-of-the-art methods. The findings support combining specialized encoders with an explicit separation objective when predicting human-perceived quality without a clean reference.
neurips-2024-learning-disentangled-repre.tldr: DisPA separates point-cloud content from distortion using specialized encoders and mutual-information minimization to improve reference-free quality assessment.

paragraphs: The shape of a heartbeat across ECG leads carries information about cardiac condition, but noise, artifacts, and missing leads can make it difficult to analyze. This paper introduces BeatDiff, a lightweight diffusion model designed to represent heartbeat morphology across multiple leads. Its learned representation becomes a foundation for several reconstruction and analysis tasks.

The authors formulate those tasks as conditional generation within a Bayesian inverse-problem framework. BeatDiff supplies the prior over heartbeat shapes, while the available measurements provide the information to condition on. An expectation-maximization algorithm, EM-BeatDiff, solves these conditional generation problems without fine-tuning the diffusion model for each task.

The demonstrated applications include removing baseline wander and electrode-motion artifacts, reconstructing a 12-lead ECG from a single lead, and unsupervised explainable anomaly detection. Single-lead reconstruction is presented as useful for smartwatch-related ECG reconstruction experiments. Numerical evaluations show the combined methods outperforming state-of-the-art approaches on the problems studied. The shared framework matters because one model of heartbeat morphology supports several tasks involving incomplete, noisy, or otherwise indirect observations.
neurips-2024-leveraging-an-ecg-beat-diff.tldr: BeatDiff and EM-BeatDiff use a shared diffusion prior to reconstruct and analyze ECG heartbeats without task-specific fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Medical language-model benchmarks often emphasize factual questions and descriptive reasoning. Clinical work also involves calculations governed by equations and explicit rules. MedCalc-Bench evaluates this quantitative capability, asking whether a model can move from information in a patient note to a requested medical value through the correct calculation.

The evaluation set contains more than 1,000 manually reviewed examples spanning 55 medical calculation tasks. Each example includes a patient note, a calculation question, a reference answer, and a step-by-step explanation of how to obtain it. This structure makes the benchmark about a complete reasoning process, including selecting information and applying the appropriate computational procedure.

The evaluated models show potential, but the authors find none effective enough for clinical settings. Common errors occur at several stages: extracting the wrong entities, selecting an incorrect equation or rule, and making arithmetic mistakes. These findings identify distinct quantitative reasoning gaps that general medical question-answering evaluations may not capture. The benchmark provides a public resource for measuring progress on those calculation tasks and examining where the process breaks down.
neurips-2024-medcalc-bench-evaluating-la.tldr: MedCalc-Bench tests medical calculations from patient notes and finds that the evaluated language models are not effective enough for clinical use.

paragraphs: Learning in a multi-agent game is difficult because outcomes depend on both the environment and the strategies of other players. Uncertainty about opponents can contribute to slow or unstable training. This paper uses imitation learning to predict opponents' next moves, aiming to reduce that uncertainty during the learning process.

The proposed imitation model works with local observations even when opponents' actions are hidden. This is central to its intended use: anticipating other players must be possible from the information available to the agent. The authors then integrate the prediction model with policy learning in a single multi-agent reinforcement-learning training process.

Combining opponent prediction and policy training makes anticipating other agents part of learning how to act. The authors evaluate the approach in three challenging game environments, including SMACv2, an advanced StarCraft multi-agent challenge. Their experiments report better performance than state-of-the-art multi-agent reinforcement-learning methods. These findings support the usefulness of the integrated approach in the evaluated games, particularly the idea that learning about opponents can help agents handle the uncertainty created by their strategies.
neurips-2024-mimicking-to-dominate-imita.tldr: The method jointly trains opponent-action prediction and agent policies to improve performance in the evaluated multi-agent games.

paragraphs: A prediction score and the decision made from it can have different fairness properties. This paper studies the gap introduced when a score is converted into a binary decision through thresholding. It introduces the margin complement, a quantity measuring the change associated with that conversion, to examine how decision-making can amplify disparities.

The authors decompose differences in an optimal binary predictor between groups into causal influences on the prediction score and on the margin complement. The decomposition distinguishes direct, indirect, and spurious pathways. Under suitable causal assumptions, influences on the squared-error-optimal score equal influences on the true outcome, allowing the analysis to separate disparities inherited from real-world outcomes from those arising through optimization.

This conditional result gives a way to examine where disparities enter the prediction-to-decision pipeline. The paper also defines weak and strong business necessity and provides an algorithm for assessing them. Applications to three real-world datasets yield insights into bias amplification. The work's practical message is that evaluating the score alone may miss disparities introduced when that score becomes a decision.
neurips-2024-mind-the-gap-a-causal-persp.tldr: A causal decomposition examines how thresholding prediction scores can introduce or amplify group disparities in final decisions.

paragraphs: Aligning language models for helpfulness and safety can be formulated as reinforcement learning with safety constraints. A common optimization approach repeatedly updates both the policy and the variables that enforce those constraints. This paper targets the computational cost and instability of that repeated primal-dual procedure.

The authors use dualization to convert the constrained alignment problem into an equivalent unconstrained one. They first optimize a dual function that is smooth, convex, and available in closed form. This preliminary optimization supplies a shortcut that removes the need for cumbersome alternating policy and dual updates, reducing the burden of the alignment procedure.

The approach produces two practical algorithms: MoCAN for model-based settings and PeCAN for preference-based settings. A broad range of experiments demonstrates their effectiveness and benefits, with the paper reporting reduced computational burden and improved training stability. The contribution concerns how safety-constrained alignment is optimized: handling the dual problem in advance makes the subsequent alignment problem simpler to solve while preserving the stated equivalence to the constrained formulation.
neurips-2024-one-shot-safety-alignment-f.tldr: Pre-optimizing a closed-form convex dual function turns safety-constrained alignment into an equivalent unconstrained problem with more stable, less costly optimization.

paragraphs: Model merging combines models fine-tuned for different tasks into a single model without retraining on their original datasets. A central difficulty is deciding how their parameter changes should interact when tasks conflict or share structure. PCB-Merging addresses this by balancing contributions at the level of individual parameters.

The method uses two assessments. Intra-balancing measures a parameter's significance within a task, while inter-balancing examines similarities across tasks. Parameters assigned low importance are removed, and the remaining parameters are rescaled to form the merged model. This makes the treatment of each parameter depend on both its role in an individual task and its relationship to other tasks.

PCB-Merging is presented as lightweight and training-free. The authors evaluate cross-task, cross-domain, and cross-training merging, along with generalization outside the evaluated models' domains. They report improvements over existing merging methods across multiple modalities, domains, model sizes, task counts, fine-tuning forms, and large language models. The findings support parameter-specific balancing as a useful way to manage competing contributions when combining specialized models into one.
neurips-2024-parameter-competition-balan.tldr: PCB-Merging combines task-specialized models by dropping and rescaling parameters according to their within-task importance and cross-task similarities.

paragraphs: Recurrent networks pass information through a sequence of steps, creating long paths for distant information and difficulties with gradients and sequential execution. The Parallel Gated Network, or PGN, changes that structure by extracting historical information directly and using gates to select and combine it with information from the current time step.

Its Historical Information Extraction layer reduces the information propagation path to constant order. The authors build on PGN with Temporal PGN, a forecasting framework containing two branches. One uses PGN to model long-term periodic patterns while retaining local characteristics. The other works with patches to capture short-term information and assemble a global representation of the series.

This division gives long-range and short-range patterns dedicated roles within the same forecasting framework. The paper reports theoretical complexity of O(√L) for TPGN and evaluates it on five benchmark datasets. The experiments show state-of-the-art forecasting performance and high efficiency. These results support PGN as an alternative to recurrent processing for the studied long-range forecasting tasks, linking a shorter information path with a design that captures patterns at multiple temporal scales.
neurips-2024-pgn-the-rnn-s-new-successor.tldr: PGN directly accesses historical information through gating, and its two-branch TPGN framework delivers efficient long-range forecasting in benchmark experiments.

paragraphs: Consistency models aim to accelerate generation from diffusion models, but applying them to high-resolution images guided by text in latent space remains challenging. This paper examines latent consistency models and identifies three flaws in their design. The authors investigate those problems and introduce Phased Consistency Models, or PCMs, as a broader design that addresses them.

PCMs are designed specifically for refinement across multiple generation steps. This makes performance over a range of step counts central to the proposal. In the reported evaluations, PCMs outperform latent consistency models from one through sixteen steps, showing improvements across both very short generation and settings that allow additional refinement.

Despite their emphasis on multiple steps, PCMs also achieve one-step results comparable to earlier state-of-the-art methods built specifically for one-step generation. The authors extend the methodology to video and report training a state-of-the-art few-step text-to-video generator. Together, these findings suggest that the proposed design supports effective refinement without sacrificing competitive one-step performance, and that its usefulness extends beyond still-image generation in the evaluated applications.
neurips-2024-phased-consistency-models-f.tldr: Phased Consistency Models improve evaluated one-to-sixteen-step image generation and extend to few-step text-to-video generation.

paragraphs: Unordered data structures, including multisets and graphs, require compression methods that respect the object being represented without losing information. This paper presents a general lossless method based on shuffle coding. Its main advance is practical efficiency: the proposed variant is many orders of magnitude faster than the original approach.

The method also supports one-shot compression of a single unordered object. This makes an individual graph or multiset a direct target for the compressor. The combination of generality and single-object operation matters because the method is presented as applicable across unordered data types, with an implementation that can be adapted to different statistical models.

The reported evaluations achieve state-of-the-art compression rates on various large network graphs while processing data at megabytes per second. The method also handles a multi-gigabyte graph containing one billion edges. These results establish both compactness and practical scale in the evaluated graph settings. The contribution is therefore a usable form of shuffle coding that combines lossless representation, substantially improved speed, and support for very large individual objects.
neurips-2024-practical-shuffle-coding-1e.tldr: A faster shuffle-coding method losslessly compresses individual unordered objects and achieves strong compression on large network graphs.

paragraphs: A coreset is a small subset of training data whose loss approximates the full dataset's loss across the parameter space. This paper asks whether sampling with determinantal point processes can produce fundamentally smaller coresets than independent sampling. These processes allow controllable negative dependence between selected points and support tractable sampling.

The authors prove that DPP-based coresets can outperform independently sampled ones. Their key observation is that coreset loss can be treated as a linear statistic of the random selection. This connects the coreset question to concentration inequalities, which describe how tightly such random quantities remain around their expected behavior.

The resulting concentration bounds cover a broad class of DPPs, including general non-projection kernels and even non-symmetric kernels. The paper also extends its treatment to vector-valued objectives. These contributions matter at two levels: they establish that dependence between selected examples can yield smaller coresets, and they expand the mathematical tools available for analyzing DPPs. The claim is that DPPs can provably improve on independent sampling, rather than that every DPP selection is always better.
neurips-2024-small-coresets-via-negative.tldr: New concentration results show that determinantal point processes can provably produce smaller coresets than independent sampling.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts models expand model capacity with relatively little additional training computation, but their size and communication patterns make deployment difficult. This paper examines language modeling and machine translation workloads to identify inference inefficiencies. It proposes three optimizations: dynamic gating, expert buffering, and expert load balancing.

Dynamic gating produces substantial improvements in maximum throughput in the reported evaluations: 6.21–11.55 times for language modeling, 5.75–10.98 times for translation encoders, and 2.58–5.71 times for translation decoders. It also reduces memory usage, with reported reduction factors of up to 1.36 for language modeling and 1.1 for translation. These measurements show benefits across distinct parts of the evaluated workloads.

Expert buffering addresses memory placement by keeping frequently active experts in GPU memory and storing the others in CPU memory. The authors report a 1.47-fold reduction in static memory allocation. Expert load balancing adds robustness to workload behavior. Together, the techniques address routing, memory residency, and workload distribution, showing how several deployment concerns can be managed within the same effort to make expert models more efficient at inference.
neurips-2024-toward-efficient-inference-.tldr: Dynamic gating, expert buffering, and load balancing improve throughput, memory use, and robustness for evaluated mixture-of-experts inference workloads.

paragraphs: A vision Transformer that performs well on familiar data may behave differently under distribution shifts. This paper introduces OoD-ViT-NAS, a benchmark of 3,000 architectures across different computational budgets, evaluated on large-scale out-of-distribution datasets. The benchmark supports studying how architectural choices affect generalization beyond the training distribution.

The analysis finds that architecture has a considerable effect on out-of-distribution performance and that in-distribution accuracy may be a poor guide to it. The authors also evaluate nine training-free architecture-search methods. These methods are largely ineffective at predicting out-of-distribution accuracy despite their usefulness for predicting accuracy on familiar data. Simple parameter-count or computation-count proxies perform better in that comparison.

The paper further reports that increasing embedding dimensions generally improves out-of-distribution generalization within the benchmark. Together, the findings indicate that architecture selection needs evidence about shifted data, since success under familiar conditions may not transfer. The benchmark provides a common basis for examining those relationships and developing search methods that account for them, while the observed trends describe the evaluated architectures and shifts.
neurips-2024-vision-transformer-neural-a.tldr: A benchmark of 3,000 vision Transformers shows that architecture strongly affects distribution-shift performance and familiar-data accuracy can be a poor guide.

paragraphs: Describing an intended image edit precisely can be difficult, even when a suitable visual reference is available. This paper proposes imitative editing: a user selects a region to change and supplies a reference image, while the system determines which reference information is relevant. The design allows inspiration from everyday images without requiring the user to resolve their fit with the source.

MimicBrush learns this behavior from video. During training, it selects two frames from a clip, masks regions in one frame, and learns to reconstruct those regions using the other. Built from a diffusion prior, the model uses this self-supervised task to learn semantic correspondences between separate images.

The training setup connects reference-based editing with recovering missing visual content from a related view. That relationship is the basis for learning what to transfer when the source and reference differ. Experiments across various test cases demonstrate the method's effectiveness and report advantages over existing alternatives. The authors also introduce a benchmark, providing a shared evaluation resource for further research on this form of image editing.
neurips-2024-zero-shot-image-editing-wit.tldr: MimicBrush learns correspondences between video frames to edit selected image regions using visual references.
